question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
Got it! 🐾

At **Norfolk Southern**, Matt’s initial rollout of the Cloud Innovation Center’s working practices did not prevent a quality crisis. Pair programming, test-first development, and continuous integration were in place from the start, but the follow-up discipline was missing. A couple of months into the engagement, the client reported rising defects while dashboards showed near-complete test coverage.

An engineer had been solutioning from his own interpretation instead of the backlog story and writing tests after the code. The backlog also contained vague stories without defined scenarios or a definition of done. The failure was not just the engineer’s: Matt had implemented the practices without consistently reinforcing and verifying them. The credibility hit landed in front of the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery.

Matt took ownership rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite, showed the gaps openly, and rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories. He brought in frontend and backend TDD experts to work alongside the engineers, using an “I do, we do, you do” progression. He also restructured agile ceremonies to keep stakeholders, developers, and product managers working from the same requirements.

Afterward, pairs rotated daily, test cases became a discrete step before engineering the solution, and adherence was checked at standup rather than inferred from dashboards. New engineers paired with seasoned practitioners.

The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see, and the failure mode did not recur after the experts left. Matt’s stated lesson was that “implementing a practice is the easy half,” with reinforcement, follow-up, and verification previously missing.

Matt’s experience includes Execution & Delivery, Org & Working-Model Transformation, and Talent & Enablement. The delivery work also crossed enterprise contexts. At **JP Morgan**, teams outpaced peer velocity within the first **two sprints**, shipping working code to production in weeks rather than months. At **Norfolk Southern**, teams reduced meeting overhead and context switching while improving velocity over successive iterations. Across the CIC, **10-person** balanced teams delivered equivalent output to traditional **20-person** teams, with **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments.

Those are Matt’s documented responsibilities and results. They do not establish that he is better than an unspecified in-house candidate, or that he owned a single enterprise product throughout its entire lifecycle. They establish that he built and operated an engineering organization—not only advised client teams.

Pairing and test-first remained the default after the experts left, and the failure mode did not recur.

He also led a **6-month** enablement program at **Norfolk Southern**. Client contributors paired into the new-state build, learned modern technologies, and took ownership of their backlog and priorities. They left with the skills to support and manage the application after **Accenture** rolled off.

Those are the facts to compare with an in-house candidate’s record: operating accountability, organizational scale, production delivery, and what remained after the engagement ended.

🐾 Here’s the failure Matt describes when asked this question.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. Instead of verifying those controls, he assumed they were correct. He focused on delivery pressures, relied on inherited documentation without confirming its accuracy, and did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes. He also did not implement compensating controls such as data masking or email interception, or verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They worked collectively to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. The root cause was insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed—assumptions Matt should have verified rather than inherited.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt describes that as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” Following the incident, IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

answer_md:
🐾 Here's a great example.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, Matt was Technology Delivery Lead for the payment engine behind ACCESS Next Generation. The bank was building on Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform, but its **135,000+** clients across **180+** countries needed payment modules, security controls, and workflows beyond the out-of-box offering. Regional legacy systems also had different data models, entitlement structures, and transaction histories that had to be consolidated without interrupting live payments.

Matt managed a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and the bank, spending **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices. Rather than treating ACCESS as a standard platform deployment, he managed the build-versus-configure boundary and delivered purpose-built ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and tax payment modules. Each had distinct formatting, validation, compliance, and workflow requirements. He implemented Message Authentication Code payment verification, payment-type-specific permissions, sanctions screening, and risk-based approval controls. For migration, he coordinated data verification with compliance teams, introduced compliance dashboards, and owned production validation and defect triage. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**; the migration completed **without disruption to live payment operations**.

At **American Express**, his payments work focused on adoption of the Virtual Payments Platform. Clients lacked SDKs, usable documentation, and a sandbox. Matt co-created a developer portal, developed Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, and built a secure sandbox with refreshed client data. He also introduced environment virtualization, Lean Product and XP practices, and a Client Onboarding Test Drive. answer_md:

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center, Matt encountered teams waiting for direction even though the center had been designed flat from day one: autonomy at the team level, collective ownership, and minimal middle layers. He supported lean, low-stakes experiments using structured hypotheses and controlled iterations, so teams could test approaches without committing to a large build.

Decentralized decision-making removed bottlenecks, and teams reported higher engagement and satisfaction. answer_md:
🐾 Here’s an example from **Norfolk Southern**.

In early **2020**, Matt’s Cloud Innovation Center team was modernizing the client’s legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A couple of months into the engagement, as the pandemic pushed the team into fully remote work, the client reported rising defects despite dashboards showing near-complete test coverage. The concerns landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery.

Matt took ownership of the failure rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and showed the gaps openly. An engineer had been building from his own interpretation instead of the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. The backlog also lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done, leaving no clear way to test the requirements.

Matt rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories. He brought frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work alongside the engineers and redo the code and tests properly. Coaching followed an “I do, we do, you do” progression, supported by coding katas, practice learning sessions, and product management training.

He then reinforced the practices beyond the initial intervention. Pairs rotated daily, newer engineers worked with seasoned practitioners, and writing test cases became a visible step before engineering the solution, checked at standup. Stories entered sprints only when testable and small enough for a **1-week** iteration.

Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. The practices held after the experts left, and the failure mode that caused the crisis did not recur.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s the story of Matt’s work at **Norfolk Southern**.

As a Director at **Accenture**, Matt led the Cloud Innovation Center’s first engagement: modernizing **Norfolk Southern’s** Revenue and Shipment Planning platform without stopping the railroad. Its mainframe dated to the **1970s**. Orders could fall out unnoticed until customers called, business rules lived in COBOL and assembly maintained by a shrinking workforce, and clerks manually handled waybill and rating fallout. The client organization was accustomed to mainframe thinking, account leadership to waterfall delivery, and the team was learning a new working model during the transition to remote work.

Rather than attempt a big-bang replacement, Matt led event storming and domain-driven design sessions, then built a hybrid platform. The mainframe remained the system of record while APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB rose beside it. Change data capture synchronized the platforms; reconciliation checked that nothing was lost. API gateways, anti-corruption layers, and structured SNAP-E documentation supported the incremental migration.

When the client grew restless for tangible progress, Matt brought revenue management into the innovation hub to co-create. The team developed the Shipper Revenue System workspace through personas, prototypes, and weekly build-measure-learn iterations. EDI validation caught malformed orders at the front door rather than waiting for customer complaints.

The work also required a quality reset. When defects rose despite near-complete test coverage, Matt audited the code and tests, found tests written after code and vague backlog stories, and introduced testable stories, TDD coaching, and coding katas. He also led a **2-day** CIC Academy course, delivered twice monthly over **6 months**, and used pairing to spread scarce legacy knowledge.

The MVP launched covering **95%** of its targeted use cases, capturing real orders with clean data feeding the mainframe. The client began co-creating in weekly iterations, and the engagement scaled to **3** balanced teams.

🐾 Found it!

At **Norfolk Southern**, billing clerks manually shepherded waybill and rating problems through green-screen consoles. Orders could disappear unnoticed until customers called. Business rules lived in COBOL and assembly maintained by a shrinking workforce. Matt had to modernize that revenue engine without stopping live rail operations, while revenue management worked in mainframe terms, account leadership expected waterfall, and his team moved into remote work during COVID.

Matt started with domain-driven design and event storming to map embedded business functions, data flows, and dependencies. Rather than attempt a wholesale replacement, he kept the mainframe as the system of record while APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB rose beside it. Change data capture synchronized the platforms; reconciliation checked that nothing was lost. Components were replaced incrementally, with API gateways and anti-corruption layers maintaining interoperability.

When the client grew restless for tangible progress, Matt brought revenue management into the innovation hub to co-create the Shipper Revenue System interface. Weekly build-measure-learn iterations moved from personas and user flows to validated prototypes. Billing clerks and shippers gained a workspace to audit and clean malformed waybill data before it caused downstream pricing errors.

A quality crisis interrupted delivery: defects were rising despite near-complete test coverage. Matt took ownership, audited the code and tests, and found tests written after code against vague backlog stories. He rebuilt the stories with defined scenarios and a definition of done, brought in TDD experts for hands-on coaching, and made test cases a visible step before implementation.

Pairing also addressed thin-stretched domain experts. Matt used “I do, we do, you do,” rotating knowledge through the team. Remote pairs traded drivers frequently to reduce fatigue; client contributors learned Angular, Node, Spring Boot, and cloud-native concepts while building the application.

The MVP covered **95%** of targeted use cases. EDI validation notified trading partners proactively instead of waiting for complaints. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see, pairing and test-first held after the experts left, and client contributors gained the skills to support the new application themselves.

question: How long did that take?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s what Matt worked on at **Norfolk Southern**.

As a Director at **Accenture**’s Cloud Innovation Center, Matt led modernization of the railroad’s Revenue and Shipment Planning platform—the CIC’s first engagement. Its mainframe dated to the **1970s**. Orders could fall out unnoticed until customers called, business rules lived in COBOL and assembly maintained by a shrinking workforce, and clerks manually handled waybill and rating fallout. Modernization had to happen without stopping rail operations, while client teams worked through mainframe thinking, account leadership expected waterfall delivery, and the pandemic forced remote work.

Rather than a big-bang replacement, Matt led a hybrid platform: the mainframe remained the system of record while APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB rose beside it. Change data capture and reconciliation kept the systems synchronized and checked that nothing was lost. Domain-driven design, event storming, the Boris Exercise, and SNAP-E documentation mapped business domains and dependencies. The team incrementally replaced components using the Strangler pattern, with Docker, Kubernetes, and automated CI/CD supporting the new services.

When the client grew restless for tangible progress, Matt brought revenue management into the innovation hub to co-create the Shipper Revenue System workspace. Personas, user flows, and prototypes became weekly build-measure-learn iterations. The MVP launched covering **95%** of its targeted use cases. EDI validation moved fallout detection from customers calling to proactive trading-partner notifications.

The work also included a quality course correction. When defects rose despite near-complete test coverage, Matt audited the code and tests rather than defending the dashboard. He rebuilt vague backlog stories, brought in TDD experts, and used Samman coaching, coding katas, and pairing. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see.

Matt also led a **2-day** CIC Academy course, delivered twice monthly over **6 months**. Pairing rotated scarce legacy knowledge through the team, while client contributors learned Angular, Node, Spring Boot, and cloud-native practices to support the application after **Accenture** rolled off.

answer_md:

The railroad’s revenue engine ran on a mainframe dating to the **1970s**. Orders could disappear unnoticed until customers called. Matt addressed the integration experience rather than simply adding platform features: cross-stack SDKs, use case-driven API documentation, a secure sandbox, and virtualized environments that reduced downstream testing dependencies. answer_md:
🐾 Perfect, here's what I found.

At **Norfolk Southern**, Matt led Revenue and Shipment Planning modernization as a Director on the Cloud Innovation Center’s first engagement. Core scheduling, billing, and order-to-cash ran on a mainframe dating to the **1970s**. Orders could fall out unnoticed until customers called, business rules lived in COBOL and assembly maintained by a shrinking workforce, and clerks manually resolved waybill and rating fallout through green-screen consoles. The railroad had to keep running throughout modernization.

Matt led domain-driven design and event storming sessions to map business functions, data flows, and dependencies. Rather than attempt a wholesale replacement, his team built APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB alongside the mainframe, which remained the system of record. Change data capture synchronized the platforms; reconciliation checked that nothing was lost. API gateways and anti-corruption layers supported incremental replacement, while Docker, Kubernetes, and automated CI/CD pipelines supported the new services. SNAP-E documentation captured APIs, dependencies, data flows, and risks.

When the client grew restless for tangible progress, Matt brought the revenue management team into the innovation hub to co-create the Shipper Revenue System UI. They worked from personas through high-fidelity prototypes in weekly build-measure-learn iterations. He also led a **2-day** CIC Academy course, delivered twice monthly over **6 months**. Pair programming addressed both resistance and scarce domain knowledge: experts worked through “I do, we do, you do,” then rotated that knowledge through the team.

The MVP launched covering **95%** of its targeted use cases, capturing real orders with clean data feeding the mainframe. EDI validation moved fallout detection from customer complaints to proactive trading-partner notifications. Delivery scaled to **3** balanced teams, and client contributors learned Angular, Node, Spring Boot, and cloud-native concepts to support the application after **Accenture** rolled off. The modernization also reduced maintenance expenses and accelerated deployment cycles, although those outcomes were not quantified.

question: Tell me about his Norfolk Southern work.

answer_md:
🐾 On it!

At **RBC**, Matt worked as Senior Technology Architecture Manager on corporate banking modernization, including program governance, architecture assessment, mobile readiness, and data conversion planning. The bank’s existing systems had performance and scalability limitations and lacked digital offerings. **RBC** was evaluating Bottomline WebSeries as the payment hub engine for its Day**2Day** Corporate Banking platform to replace the aging **RBC** Express portal.

A central question was whether WebSeries could actually meet the bank’s requirements before further investment. Matt conducted code reviews, stakeholder interviews, and documentation analysis. He assessed Data, Application, Technology, and Business Architecture, created architectural heat maps, and worked with the enterprise architecture team on target-system models and cost-to-fix versus benefit comparisons. The assessment found that WebSeries lacked the modularity required for **RBC**’s long-term digital operating model. The bank avoided further investment in that platform path and redirected technical resources toward higher-priority initiatives.

Matt also established the PMO during discovery and requirements. He developed the project management plan, maintained the program roadmap and dependencies, and consolidated financial, quality, resource, and project reporting. A shared communication platform, daily summaries, designated team contacts, and a task-tracking matrix coordinated work across **3 organizations**: **RBC**, **Accenture**, and Bottomline Technologies. The resulting framework eliminated missed program updates and reduced redundant efforts.

When the previous data conversion lead left early in the initiative, Matt took over the workstream from scratch. He delivered a conversion plan covering legacy payment-data analysis, source-to-target transformation rules, mock conversion cycles, and reconciliation of payment amounts and beneficiary details. He also delivered a mobile modernization blueprint defining API integration, cheque deposit capabilities, and cross-device scalability requirements.

The documented outcomes were the investment decision, resource redirection, governance framework, and modernization and conversion plans. Dollar savings and delivery-speed improvements were not quantified.
